p4c4.essay:
He comes at eleven at night to say 'one word' and takes the whole chapter not to say it. That is the first thing I would hold on to: this is a confession scene in which the confession does not occur. What happens instead is an interrogation, then a reading, then a proposal, and each is stranger than the last.

The interrogation first, because it is easy to take for mere cruelty. Raskolnikov walks Sonia through her own future with a prosecutor's patience (the hospital, the children in the street, Polenka on the same road) and tops it with 'perhaps, there is no God at all.' It is cruel; the narrator says so outright, calling him 'young, abstract, and therefore cruel,' one of the few times this book passes sentence on its hero in plain words. But watch what he is testing. He needs Sonia to be like him: someone who stepped over a line by an act of will and now has to live on the far side of it. If she is, he has company. So he lists her three exits, 'the canal, the madhouse, or... depravity,' and they are, not by accident, the exits he has been pacing in front of himself since [[p2c6|the evening on the bridge]]. When none of them fits her, he reaches for a diagnosis: 'religious maniac.' He 'liked that explanation indeed better than any other,' and Dostoevsky lets us hear the liking. A man who has an explanation for everything meets something he cannot explain, and madness is the last category he has left.

What he cannot get round is how she talks. Ask her about her own ruin and she tells you about a pair of embroidered collars she was too mean to give away. Katerina Ivanovna, who by Marmeladov's account in [[p1c2]] pushed her onto the street, is 'like a child,' 'seeking righteousness.' Sonia's compassion is called 'insatiable.' The narrator apologises for the word and it is the right one: an appetite, not a principle. Raskolnikov's theory runs on arithmetic, one life weighed against a hundred. Sonia cannot do the sum. She is not refuting him; she simply has no faculty for it.

Then the book on the chest of drawers. Notice whose it was. The New Testament came from Lizaveta, Sonia had a requiem sung for Lizaveta, the two of them used to read together; so when Raskolnikov says 'You used to read to Lizaveta,' he is asking to sit in his own victim's chair. I find that almost unbearable, and I think he half knows what he is doing. He asks for Lazarus by name. Porfiry put that very question to him in [[p3c5]], whether he believed in the raising of Lazarus literally, and he said yes a little too quickly. Now he wants to hear it from someone for whom it is not a debating point.

The reading is the centre of the novel as I read it, and Dostoevsky does something bold: he simply prints the Gospel, verse after verse, and puts the drama in the stage directions. Her voice breaks 'like an overstrained string,' then rings 'like a bell'; she reads Martha's 'Yea, Lord: I believe' as her own public confession; she leans on the word 'four.' Four days dead and already stinking: the point of this miracle is that it comes too late by any reasonable reckoning. And the man listening lives in a room his mother called a tomb, and has hidden what he stole under a stone. Nobody in the scene says so. The text is laid beside him and left there.

And it does not work, not here. Sonia is 'quivering with happy anticipation' that he will believe 'at once, now,' and what she gets, five minutes later, is 'Freedom and power, and above all, power!' He claims her as a fellow transgressor ('it's all the same!' It is not the same, and the parenthesis knows it), speaks in one breath of children as 'the image of Christ' and of mastery over 'the ant-heap,' and leaves with a promise for tomorrow. Compassion and Napoleon are both still in him, unreconciled, a few lines apart in the same speech.

Two smaller things. The landlord's name, Kapernaumov, carries Capernaum in it, the town of the Gospel healings, and his household is all lame and stammering, a little parish of the unhealed around Sonia's door. And the last paragraph. After all that candlelight Dostoevsky turns the scene inside out: someone has been standing on the other side of the locked door the whole time, and has 'greatly enjoyed it.' The most private hour in the book had an audience. I laughed the first time, at the chair, and then stopped laughing.

annotations.quote: In the opposite side on the right hand wall was another door, always kept locked.
annotations.note: Dostoevsky is not a novelist who describes rooms for the pleasure of it, so when he stops to count the doors, count them with him. The crooked room, one corner too sharp and one too blunt, is also the first interior in the book that belongs to Sonia, and it is as misshapen as the life she has been pushed into.

annotations.quote: And she was not grieved for the collars, but for my refusing, I saw that.
annotations.note: Asked about her degradation, Sonia confesses to this: being stingy over a set of collars. Her scale of sin is entirely different from his, measured in small unkindnesses. And look who sold her the collars. Lizaveta's name enters the room here, quietly, in a story about haberdashery, and Raskolnikov's next question shows he heard it.

annotations.quote: “But, perhaps, there is no God at all,” Raskolnikov answered with a sort of malignance, laughed and looked at her.
annotations.note: The three verbs matter more than the sentence he speaks. He says it, laughs, and then looks to see what it did. This is an experiment on a person, and it is the ugliest moment in the chapter. Her answer is not an argument, only 'unutterable reproach' and tears, and it visibly shakes him more than an argument would have.

annotations.quote: “I did not bow down to you, I bowed down to all the suffering of humanity,”
annotations.note: Even on his knees he generalises. He has just kissed the foot of a particular frightened girl, and within a breath he has turned her into a symbol. Sonia's question, 'What are you doing to me?', is the better one: she insists on being a person to whom things are done. The gap between loving humanity and seeing the human in front of you is this novel's steady subject.

annotations.quote: he was a sceptic, he was young, abstract, and therefore cruel
annotations.note: A rare verdict from the narrator in his own voice, and the 'therefore' is the whole of it. Cruelty here is not a vice of temperament but a consequence of abstraction: think in categories for long enough and people become cases. It is as close as Dostoevsky comes to stating the diagnosis outright.

annotations.quote: “She is a religious maniac!” he repeated to himself.
annotations.note: Garnett's phrase is clinical, and it loses something. The Russian word is the one for a holy fool, the 'fool for Christ' whom Russian tradition half fears and half reveres. So in the original he reaches for an insult and, without meaning to, hands her a title. Notice too how eagerly he repeats it. He needs her faith to be an illness.

annotations.quote: She laid emphasis on the word _four_.
annotations.note: Why this word? I think because four days is the detail that makes the miracle unreasonable. It is not a rescue from a sickbed but from decay: 'by this time he stinketh.' Sonia is reading to a man she believes is far gone, and she wants him to hear that far gone is exactly the case the story is about.

annotations.quote: the murderer and the harlot who had so strangely been reading together the eternal book
annotations.note: The most quoted sentence in the chapter and the most argued over. Nabokov thought it a piece of cheap rhetoric, yoking a killer and a prostitute as if their cases were alike. I half agree that the flourish is stagey, but the yoking is Raskolnikov's own idea, pressed a page later, and I read the sentence as showing us the tableau he wants to see. The guttering candle-end is better than the epithets.

annotations.quote: You, too, have transgressed... have had the strength to transgress.
annotations.note: The Russian verb means to step over, and it shares its root with the word for 'crime' in the title; Garnett's 'transgressed' (Latin for stepping across) keeps the echo. It is the vocabulary of his article in [[p3c5]]. See what he is doing: recruiting her sacrifice into his theory, as though selling yourself to feed children and killing to prove a point were one act of 'strength.'

annotations.quote: brought a chair and noiselessly carried it to the door that led to Sonia’s room
annotations.note: The chair is the touch of genius. Not a villain's start of horror at what he has overheard, but a man arranging his comfort for the next instalment. We last saw Svidrigailov discover he was Sonia's neighbour at the end of [[p3c4]]; that small coincidence has just come due.

links.why: Marmeladov's tavern monologue is where Raskolnikov first heard of Sonia, the Kapernaumovs and the six-to-nine walk he throws back at her here.
Porfiry asked him point-blank whether he believed in the raising of Lazarus; tonight he asks to hear it read.
Sonia's visit to his room, and the gentleman who followed her home afterwards and found they were neighbours.
The canal as a way out: he stood on the bridge and weighed the same three exits he now lists for her.

p4c5.essay:
After the candle, the office: yellow government furniture, clerks who do not look up, and ten minutes of being made to wait. I love that Dostoevsky sets these two interviews back to back. Last night Raskolnikov was the interrogator, pacing the room and pressing a frightened person with hypotheticals until she wept. This morning it is done to him, by a man who paces faster.

Porfiry's method is to describe his method. That is the chapter's joke and its terror. Raskolnikov opens by sneering at the textbook trick (lull the suspect with trivia, then the 'knock-down blow') and Porfiry agrees delightedly, adopts the phrase, credits him with witticisms he never made, and then explains, purely in the abstract, about 'a man' of 'our sort,' exactly why he has not arrested him. Leave such a man free and uncertain and he will circle like 'a butterfly round a candle' (we would say a moth) until he flies into your mouth. It is a strategy confessed as small talk, and it goes on working after it has been explained, because its mechanism is the hearer's nerves, and knowing about your nerves does not steady them.

What interests me most is that Porfiry is attacking the article as much as the alibi. 'The general case... does not exist at all'; every crime 'at once becomes a thoroughly special case.' The Austrian staff beat Napoleon on paper and General Mack surrendered. All of this is aimed at the young theorist of [[p3c5]] who sorted mankind into two classes: you planned it in the study, Porfiry is saying, and forgot you have a body that faints. Garnett's word is 'temperament,' the creature itself, and it is the one thing no calculation covered. The fainting fit in [[p2c1]] and the bell-ringing in [[p2c6]] both come back as evidence that is not quite evidence: psychology, which, as Porfiry is the first to admit, can 'cut both ways.'

Is he sincere when he fusses with the decanter and says 'I have a sincere liking for you'? I think the unsettling answer is partly yes. 'You believe a quarter,' he says, and a quarter seems about right. He is barely thirty-five and calls himself an old man running to seed; something in him recognises this boy.

Watch the two whispers. Twice Raskolnikov shouts, twice Porfiry hushes him, and twice he obeys and hates that he obeys. The suspect and the magistrate with their heads together, agreeing to keep it down so the clerks will not hear: that picture says more about where the power sits than any of the speeches. Then the key, the locked door, the 'little surprise,' and the chapter stops in mid-air.

annotations.quote: “He held out both hands to me, but he did not give me one--he drew it back in time,”
annotations.note: The duel begins before anyone has said anything of substance. Raskolnikov is reading gestures now the way he will read phrases a moment later ('Why did I put in I believe?'). A mind that audits its own small talk and its host's handshake is already doing the examiner's work for him.

annotations.quote: like a ball rolling from one side to the other and rebounding back
annotations.note: Porfiry is all roundness and bounce, and the comedy is deliberate camouflage. A suspect braces against a hawk. It is much harder to brace against an india-rubber ball that giggles, apologises and asks whether you would like a cigarette.

annotations.quote: The work of investigation is, so to speak, a free art in its own way, he-he-he!
annotations.note: Raskolnikov keeps demanding 'the proper form' because form would protect him: charges, questions, a record. Porfiry's answer is that he is an artist and need not be bound by it. Notice which of them is now the champion of rules and which the exceptional man who steps over them.

annotations.quote: every crime, for instance, so soon as it actually occurs, at once becomes a thoroughly special case
annotations.note: This sounds like a lawyer's shop talk and is really a rebuttal. The article Porfiry admired so slyly in [[p3c5]] dealt in categories of men and classes of act. Here he answers it in passing: once a thing is actually done, by an actual person, the category evaporates.

annotations.quote: Have you seen a butterfly round a candle? That’s how he will keep circling and circling round me.
annotations.note: Garnett's 'butterfly' is literal; in English we would call the creature a moth. The image answers a question the book has been raising since the murder: why does he keep going back, to the flat, to the police office, to conversations about the case? Porfiry calls it 'a law of nature.' I would keep that phrase in mind and ask whether nerves are the whole of the explanation.

annotations.quote: but look you, General Mack surrendered with all his army, he-he-he!
annotations.note: Mack was the Austrian general whom Napoleon surrounded at Ulm in 1805. It is a wicked choice of anecdote for this particular listener: the planners who had Napoleon beaten on paper, told to a young man with his own ideas about Napoleon. A nice accident of publishing, too: Tolstoy's novel, in which Mack turns up in person, was running in the same magazine as this one.

annotations.quote: but at the most interesting, the most flagrant moment he will faint
annotations.note: Still 'a man,' still hypothetical, and both of them know it is the faint in the police office in [[p2c1]]. Porfiry even supplies the excuse ('illness and a stuffy room') before taking it away. Then he asks whether the room is stuffy now. The cruelty is exquisite.

annotations.quote: “Hush, my dear man! They’ll hear and come in. Just think, what could we say to them?”
annotations.note: That 'we' is the masterstroke. In four words Porfiry makes himself the accomplice, the two of them with something to hide from the clerks next door. And Raskolnikov drops to a whisper. He goes on repeating 'I won't allow it' while doing exactly as he is told.

annotations.quote: why, my good sir, in your illness and in your delirium were you haunted by just those delusions and not by any others?
annotations.note: Having handed him the delirium defence, Porfiry cuts it in half. A feverish man might do anything; this one went and rang one particular bell. It is the sharpest question in the chapter and it is thrown away inside a giggle.

annotations.quote: “You are lying,” roared Raskolnikov without restraint, “you lie, you damned punchinello!”
annotations.note: Punchinello is the hook-nosed clown of the Italian comedy, the ancestor of Mr. Punch, and it suits the bouncing Porfiry rather well. It also marks the end of the vow Raskolnikov made in the waiting-room 'to keep as silent as possible.' Porfiry's reply is unanswerable: 'you could not betray yourself any further.'

links.why: The first round with Porfiry, and the article on crime that he keeps quoting back with such relish.
The night visit to the flat, the bell and the question about the blood, which Porfiry now knows about.
The faint in the police office, which Porfiry retells here as a general law of the criminal temperament.
The night before, in the same position reversed: Raskolnikov pacing and pressing, someone else in tears.

p4c6.essay:
The surprise that arrives is not the one behind the door. I think this is one of the best-built reversals in the novel, and it is worth seeing how it is made: Porfiry has spent a chapter boasting that the special case always defeats the plan, and then a special case walks in and defeats his. A pale young workman drops to his knees and says the words the whole morning was designed to draw out of somebody else.

We have heard of Nikolay before, at second hand, in Razumihin's story in [[p2c4]]: the house-painter with the earrings. Here he is in person for the first time, and what strikes me is his vocabulary. 'Mine is the sin.' 'Darkness came over me.' It is not the language of the office he is kneeling in; it sounds much more like the room on the canal last night. And Porfiry, to his credit, does not believe a word: 'It's not his own tale he is telling.' An investigator who is handed a free confession and is annoyed by it is, whatever else he may be, not a man who merely wants a conviction.

Then the comedy on the stairs, which I relish: two men who are both trembling, both admit it, and trade compliments about Gogol while promising to know each other 'through and through.' Raskolnikov believes he has won the exchange. Notice that Porfiry is the one who runs after him.

And then the second kneeling. The 'phantom sprung out of the earth' from [[p3c6]] turns out to be a tradesman who cures hides, lost sleep over a grudge, and has come to bow to the ground and beg pardon of a murderer for having thought him one. 'May God forgive you,' says Raskolnikov, and Dostoevsky lets the line stand without comment. Put these three chapters side by side and a pattern shows. Two interviews, each with a listener on a chair behind a locked door. Three people on their knees or bowing to the floor, Raskolnikov at Sonia's feet, then Nikolay, then the tradesman; and the one who actually did it is the only one who confesses nothing.

So he goes out 'more confident than ever,' the evidence dissolved into 'psychology.' But read the last sentence again. The malice is 'aimed at himself.' He is ashamed of having been afraid, not of the thing he was afraid of being caught for. And just before the visitor came he was murmuring 'To-day! To-day,' with a 'suffering smile,' thinking of what he promised Sonia. The chapter sets him free and he does not feel free.

annotations.quote: When he remembered the scene afterwards, this is how Raskolnikov saw it.
annotations.note: An odd little hinge after the cliffhanger. The narrator steps back and gives us the scene as memory, which is how something that takes thirty seconds and makes no sense would be kept. It also prepares us for an account that explains nothing: he saw it, he did not understand it.

annotations.quote: “I am guilty! Mine is the sin! I am the murderer,”
annotations.note: Three sentences, and the middle one is the strange one. Not 'I did it' but 'mine is the sin,' the language of church rather than of a deposition. Raskolnikov has spent two chapters shouting 'arrest me in due form'; this man kneels. Whatever is true about Nikolay, he and Raskolnikov do not mean the same thing by guilt.

annotations.quote: “It’s not his own tale he is telling,” he muttered as though to himself
annotations.note: Porfiry's instinct, instantly, is that the confession is recited. His questions show why: Nikolay answers too fast, 'as though he had prepared the answer,' and volunteers his state of mind before he is asked for the facts. Raskolnikov catches the mutter, and on the stairs he cannot resist showing that he caught it.

annotations.quote: “Now you’re going to a birthday party?”
annotations.note: Raskolnikov told him twenty minutes ago that he was going to a funeral. Is this a rattled man's slip, or one last small needle to see whether the suspect corrects him too quickly? I honestly cannot tell, and I suspect Dostoevsky wanted it that way. With Porfiry you never know which of the stumbles are real.

annotations.quote: They say that was the marked characteristic of Gogol, among the writers.
annotations.note: A murder suspect and his examining magistrate, both with shaking hands, pausing on a staircase to agree about Gogol. The remark is half a compliment and half a file note: Porfiry is still cataloguing this young man's mind. And Gogol is apt, since the scene they have just played, with its wrong man bursting through the door, is very nearly farce.

annotations.quote: he would have looked exactly like a peasant woman
annotations.note: Yesterday this figure was a nightmare, the stranger who said one word in the street in [[p3c6]] and vanished. Today he sighs like an old countrywoman. Dostoevsky deflates the phantom with a single homely comparison, and the deflation is its own kind of shock: the terror was real, the cause was nothing.

annotations.quote: “May God forgive you,” answered Raskolnikov.
annotations.note: The customary reply to a man who bows and asks forgiveness, and here it is spoken by the guilty to the innocent, about an accusation that was true. Raskolnikov seems not to hear what he is saying. I do not think the reader is meant to miss it, least of all the night after the scene with Sonia's New Testament.

annotations.quote: no facts but this _psychology_ which _cuts both ways_, nothing positive
annotations.note: The phrase is Porfiry's own, from the last chapter, and Raskolnikov seizes it as a shield: if every sign can be read two ways, nothing can be proved. He is right as a matter of law. But a man who comforts himself in his interrogator's vocabulary has not got that interrogator out of his head.

annotations.quote: His malice was aimed at himself; with shame and contempt he recollected his “cowardice.”
annotations.note: The quotation marks round 'cowardice' are the narrator's, and they keep a distance from the word. What he calls cowardice was fear, and perhaps something besides fear. He walks out resolved to 'make a fight for it,' but the last feeling the chapter records is contempt for himself, which is a poor thing to fight on.

links.why: Razumihin's account of Nikolay the painter and the earrings: everything we knew of him before he came through that door.
The stranger in the street, as he first appeared: one word, and then gone.
The scene in the gateway that the tradesman has been losing sleep over ever since.
Another listener on a chair behind a locked door, and the promise for 'to-day' that Raskolnikov is remembering as he reaches for his cap.
